learningObjective: Estimate effective HBM bandwidth achieved by a strided access pattern compared to the ideal coalesced case and identify the underlying mechanism.

canonicalClaims.claim: Effective useful bandwidth for a global-memory access equals useful bytes divided by total sector bytes transferred; the waste factor is (sectors_touched × sector_size) / useful_bytes.
conditions: First-touch access with no reuse from L2.
Sector granularity is the memory-system's minimum transfer unit (e.g., 32 B on recent NVIDIA GPUs).
nonImplications: Does not imply L2 or L1 can never mitigate the waste; repeated access to the same sectors amortizes it.
Does not imply that transactions are equal to sectors — coalescing can group multiple sectors into a single memory transaction.

misconceptions.claim: The number of sectors touched divides the effective bandwidth directly.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Effective bandwidth is useful bytes / total bytes moved. Total bytes = sectors × sector_size; sectors alone omit the sector size in the ratio.

misconceptions.claim: L2 caches transparently hide strided access waste on modern GPUs.
misconceptions.whyWrong: L2 helps only for repeated access; first-touch access still pulls full sectors from HBM.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA Best Practices Guide, L2 discussion

misconceptions.claim: Coalescing rules use 128 B transaction size on all recent architectures.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Recent NVIDIA GPUs use 32 B sectors at L2 as the effective granularity; the 128 B figure is a legacy or aggregate description.

implementationFacts: Stride-1 with 4 B elements: warp touches 1 × 128 B / 128 B useful = 1.0 efficiency.
Stride-32 with 4 B elements: warp touches 32 × 32 B sectors / 128 B useful = 8× waste, 1/8 efficiency.
performanceScenarios: Non-contiguous strided access (e.g., transposed matrix rows) is a common Nsight Compute finding, motivating layout transformations or shared-memory staging.
